strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision and robotics problem: metric-scale amodal reconstruction when the manipulated object is severely occluded. Using touch and known hand geometry is well motivated because these signals constrain precisely the regions where RGB evidence is absent.

The shared camera-aligned SDF representation provides a coherent way to combine image evidence, proprioception, contacts, object pose, and scale. Applying differentiable contact and non-interpenetration energies during both training and sampling is technically appealing.

The simulation evaluation spans multiple object datasets, three training end-effectors, 35 listed YCB test objects, many rendered views, several occlusion levels, and both reconstruction and pose metrics. Improvements are generally largest under severe occlusion, matching the method's motivation.

The reported simulation results are promising: compared with SAM3D, the method improves aggregate CD from 0.039 to 0.033, voxel IoU from 0.504 to 0.586, and 3D pose IoU from 0.406 to 0.530. Testing on a real robot with an unseen hand morphology is also a valuable attempt at cross-embodiment validation.

The manuscript is mostly clear, gives explicit mathematical formulations of the VAE, flow objective, physical losses, and sampling guidance, and appropriately acknowledges sensitivity to calibration, masks, grid resolution, and embodiment changes.
weaknesses: The quantitative reporting contains serious internal inconsistencies. In Table A1, every per-bin NC, F-score, voxel-IoU, and EMD value for No-Touch is exactly identical to the corresponding full-model value in Table 1, while only CD changes substantially. Several Vision-Only F-scores likewise exactly duplicate Amodal3R's values. Table 1 also reports SAM3D NC=0.081 in B3 amid neighboring values near 0.8. These apparent copy or transcription errors undermine confidence in the central evidence, especially the claimed benefit of touch.

The paper does not directly evaluate its defining physical-grounding claims. It reports no contact-distance, penetration-volume, collision-rate, grasp-feasibility, or downstream manipulation metric. Figure A3 is only qualitative, and there is no quantitative ablation of the contact loss, non-interpenetration loss, or inference-time guidance. Standard shape metrics cannot establish that reconstructions are physically feasible.

The sensing ablation does not cleanly substantiate the tactile contribution. The full model is absent from Table A1, must be cross-referenced to Table 1, and—subject to the suspicious duplicated entries—touch appears to improve only CD while leaving four metrics unchanged to three decimal places. There is also no comparison to a simple contact-based optimization of a vision-only reconstruction or to prior vision-touch reconstruction approaches.

The real-world validation is too limited and insufficiently specified for the strength of the transfer claims: it uses only five YCB objects, gives no number of trials or uncertainty, does not explain how ground-truth metric pose/alignment was obtained, and reports no real-world pose or physical-consistency measurements. The method is worse than SAM3D on real-world F-score and EMD, despite using extra sensing.

Dataset and protocol descriptions disagree: the main paper states 22,680 YCB test images, whereas the supplement reports 865 grasps and 20,760 images; the claimed 36-object subset contains only 35 listed objects. Occlusion-bin sample counts, variability across random seeds, confidence intervals, invalid-output rates, and the precise aggregation procedure are not reported.

Baseline coverage is narrow and does not isolate whether gains arise from the proposed physics formulation rather than privileged multimodal inputs. Both principal baselines are vision-only, while the proposed method receives calibrated hand geometry and touch. Comparisons to relevant vision-touch reconstruction or pose methods, and modality-matched alternative fusion strategies, are needed.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including architecture sizes, training schedules and compute, loss weights, solver step count, guidance parameters, exact stabilization/projection rules, and several preprocessing settings. Moreover, the same object-trained VAE is used to encode and decode hand SDFs without evidence that it accurately represents these out-of-distribution geometries.

The metric-scale claim is not adequately verified through explicit scale or translation error. CD/EMD units, normalization, threshold interpretation, and whether metrics are computed before or after alignment are unclear. Possible overlap or duplicates between the 100k-object pretraining corpus and YCB evaluation objects are also not addressed. Given the promising idea but unreliable tables and missing evidence for its central physical-grounding claims, the current scientific case favors rejection.

strengths: The problem is important for robotic perception: single-view reconstruction during grasping is severely underconstrained, and proprioception plus touch provide relevant evidence precisely in occluded regions.

The proposed pipeline is conceptually coherent. Camera-aligned metric SDFs place the object, hand geometry, and contacts in a shared differentiable representation, enabling both contact-consistency and non-interpenetration objectives.

The simulation results report substantial improvements over vision-only baselines under heavy occlusion, and evaluation on held-out YCB objects and an unseen real-robot end-effector is directionally encouraging.
The paper clearly describes the principal losses and acknowledges meaningful limitations involving calibration, resolution, and cross-embodiment generalization.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence contains serious internal inconsistencies. In Table A1, every per-bin NC, F-score, Voxel-IoU, and EMD value for No-Touch is exactly identical to the full model in Table 1 despite different CD values. Moreover, the reported No-Touch aggregate NC of 0.760 is below every bin value (0.803–0.868), and its aggregate Voxel-IoU of 0.430 is below every bin value (0.526–0.616), which is impossible for an ordinary sample-weighted aggregate. This undermines confidence in the core touch ablation.

Other reporting inconsistencies compound this concern: the main paper reports 22,680 test images, whereas the supplement reports 865 grasps times 24 views, i.e. 20,760 images; the listed YCB set appears to contain 35 rather than the claimed 36 objects; and SAM3D's B3 normal consistency in Table 1 is reported as 0.081, likely an order-of-magnitude error.

The experiments do not isolate the paper's main algorithmic components. There are no controlled ablations of tactile conditioning versus the contact loss, non-interpenetration loss, inference-time decoder guidance, or the SDF regularizers. Consequently, the claimed benefit of explicitly injecting physics cannot be distinguished from the benefit of providing hand geometry or from architectural/training differences.

Physical plausibility is asserted but not quantitatively evaluated. The paper reports conventional reconstruction and pose metrics, but no penetration volume/depth, contact satisfaction, collision rate, scale error, or downstream manipulation success. Figure A3 is only a single qualitative guidance trajectory.

The comparison does not cleanly establish improvement over the most relevant alternatives. The principal baselines are vision-only and therefore lack privileged hand/contact observations available to the proposed method. There is no adapted vision-touch reconstruction baseline, contact-based optimization of a strong visual reconstruction, or matched-input alternative. Differences in model capacity, training data, refinement stages, and pose inputs further complicate attribution.

The real-world study is too limited to substantiate broad sim-to-real or cross-embodiment claims: it uses only five familiar YCB instances, gives no number of trials or uncertainty, and does not provide a controlled same-hand versus unseen-hand comparison. The method also loses to SAM3D on real-world F-score and EMD despite using additional sensors.

Evaluation excludes invalid output meshes without reporting failure rates, which can bias every metric. Occlusion-bin sample counts, repeated-run variance, sampling protocol, and statistical uncertainty are also absent.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Important architecture dimensions, training schedules, loss weights, inference-guidance parameters and stabilization rules, tactile/contact distributions, metric grid extent, and Stage-B implementation details are missing even from the supplement.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the technical novelty is modest: the method primarily combines an SDF VAE, conditional flow matching, established contact/non-penetration losses, and gradient guidance. Such an integration could still be valuable, but the unreliable and incomplete experimental validation does not presently support acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision and robotics problem: metric-scale amodal reconstruction when the object is severely occluded precisely during physical interaction.

The central formulation is compelling. Camera-aligned SDFs place vision, articulated hand geometry, and tactile contacts in a common metric frame, while differentiability enables contact and non-interpenetration guidance during both training and sampling.
The method combines a learned shape prior with complementary physical evidence: proprioception constrains infeasible occupied space, whereas touch supplies localized positive surface observations.

Simulation evaluation is substantial, using 36 held-out YCB objects and over 20,000 rendered observations stratified by occlusion. Improvements are strongest under severe occlusion, matching the paper's motivation; for example, in B5 the method improves voxel IoU from 0.337 for SAM3D to 0.532.

Pose results are also encouraging: the aggregate 3D IoU improves from 0.406 to 0.530 and ICP rotation error decreases from 18.875 to 10 degrees relative to SAM3D, despite that baseline receiving ground-truth depth-derived point maps.

Deployment on a real humanoid with an unseen end-effector is valuable evidence that the shared geometric representation can transfer across embodiments. The paper also candidly identifies sensitivity to calibration, masks, grid resolution, and hand morphology.

The manuscript is generally clear, well motivated, and visually effective, and it appropriately positions Stage B as an integration demonstration rather than presenting it as the primary technical contribution.
weaknesses: The central physical-consistency claim is not evaluated directly. The paper should report contact error, penetration depth or volume, collision rate, and output validity rate. Shape metrics alone cannot establish that the contact and non-interpenetration objectives produce physically feasible reconstructions.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed physics components. There is no quantitative comparison removing the contact loss, non-interpenetration loss, decoder guidance, or individual guidance terms, so improvements cannot be attributed to the main algorithmic mechanisms rather than multimodal conditioning alone.

Table A1 contains a serious apparent reporting inconsistency: nearly every NC, F-score, voxel-IoU, and EMD entry for the No-Touch model is exactly identical to the full model in Table 1, while only CD changes. This improbable duplication undermines the key claim that touch improves reconstruction and needs correction or explanation. Table 1 also reports SAM3D NC=0.081 in B3, likely a typo given neighboring results.
Dataset counts conflict: Sec. 4.1 states 22,680 test images, whereas the supplement reports 865 grasps with 24 views, which equals 20,760 images. Such inconsistencies should be resolved.

The real-world evaluation covers only five YCB objects already represented in the simulation test set. The number of physical trials, object-wise results, variability across grasps, registration procedure for ground truth, and uncertainty estimates are omitted. Consequently, it demonstrates feasibility but provides limited evidence of robust sim-to-real or object-level generalization.
The statement that only valid output meshes are evaluated introduces possible survivorship bias, yet the valid-output rate for each method is not reported.

Reproducibility is limited by missing architectural and optimization details, including latent dimensions, model capacity, training schedules, loss weights, sampling steps, and guidance hyperparameters. The stabilization heuristics for guidance are described only at a high level.

Baseline fairness and attribution could be strengthened with a common-data vision-only baseline and a controlled model receiving identical architecture/training but successively adding hand conditioning, touch, physics losses, and guidance. The present comparisons mix different model capacities and training distributions.

The method's originality is primarily in a thoughtful integration of established SDF, latent flow-matching, multimodal conditioning, and gradient-guidance components. This is useful, but the lack of direct physical evaluation and clean component ablations keeps the evidence just below a confident accept.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant vision/robotics problem: metric-scale amodal reconstruction when the manipulating hand severely occludes the object. Using proprioception and touch as positive and negative geometric evidence is well motivated.

The shared camera-aligned SDF representation provides a coherent domain for RGB evidence, hand geometry, contacts, object pose, and differentiable physical objectives. Combining physics-aware training with decoder-based sampling guidance is technically sensible.

The simulation study is reasonably broad: it evaluates 36 held-out YCB objects over 22,680 images, stratifies results by occlusion, compares against Amodal3R and SAM3D, and reports complementary geometry and pose metrics. Improvements are especially pronounced under severe occlusion.

The ablations provide useful evidence for proprioception, touch, contact-distance encoding, physics losses, inference guidance, and robustness to several input perturbations. Testing on DexYCB and an unseen real robot hand also supports some cross-embodiment generalization.
The manuscript is generally clear, includes informative qualitative results, and candidly discusses sensitivity to calibration, fixed-grid resolution, and camera-centric coordinates.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the principal scientific claim is physical consistency, yet the experiments never quantitatively report contact error, penetration depth/volume, collision rate, or contact satisfaction. Global reconstruction and pose metrics do not establish that the generated shapes are physically feasible; the guidance evidence is mostly a single qualitative trajectory.

The real-world validation is too limited and insufficiently documented to substantiate strong deployment claims. It covers only five YCB objects, does not state the number of trials or report uncertainty, and does not explain how ground-truth real-world geometry and pose were obtained. It also uses real counterparts of simulated test objects rather than genuinely novel objects.

Evaluation is potentially biased by stating that only valid output meshes are considered without reporting reconstruction/failure rates for the principal simulation and real-world tables. Results are averaged over an unspecified number of generative seeds and contain no confidence intervals or significance analysis.

Baseline coverage does not isolate the value of the proposed physical formulation adequately. The main alternatives are vision-only, and there is no comparison to a simpler optimization/post-processing baseline that fits a vision reconstruction to the same hand and contact constraints. The paper’s own vision/no-touch ablations help, but changes in architecture, training data, pose-aware conditioning, and physical cues remain partly confounded.

Reproducibility is presently weak. Important architectural and optimization details are absent, including latent dimensions, transformer size, training schedules, loss weights, contact construction statistics, and the numerical values for guidance strength, EMA decay, normalization, trust region, and optional projection. Stage B is described only briefly, and it is unclear precisely which refinement route produces each reported result.

Some presentation and reporting issues need correction: the SAM3D normal-consistency value for bin B3 in Table 1 appears to be an erroneous 0.081; Stage-B integration into SAM3D is described as preliminary despite appearing in the pipeline discussion; and several claims of physical plausibility are stronger than the supplied measurements support. Overall, the idea and simulation results are promising, but missing evidence for the central claim and limited real-world validation slightly favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: metric-scale object reconstruction under severe hand occlusion, where vision-only methods are fundamentally ambiguous.

The integration of camera-aligned SDF generation, proprioceptive hand geometry, volumetric contact encoding, physics-aware training losses, and decoder-based inference guidance is coherent and technically interesting, even though most individual components are established.

The simulation evaluation is reasonably broad: it uses held-out YCB objects, 22,680 rendered images, multiple occlusion levels, reconstruction and pose metrics, external baselines, modality ablations, component ablations, and several input-noise tests.

The controlled ablations provide evidence that proprioception and touch are useful. For example, CD improves from 0.142 for Vision-Only to 0.085 without touch and 0.033 for the full model; removing physics losses also worsens CD from 0.033 to 0.052.

The attempt at real-robot and cross-embodiment transfer is valuable. The paper also candidly identifies sensitivity to calibration, kinematics, masks, fixed voxel resolution, and camera-aligned coordinates.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the visualizations communicate the intended pipeline and qualitative behavior effectively.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved physical plausibility is not adequately evaluated. The main experiments report conventional shape and pose metrics but no direct contact-consistency, penetration-volume, collision-rate, or physical-task metric. Better Chamfer distance or voxel IoU does not establish that reconstructions are physically feasible. The supplementary DexYCB interpenetration result is limited to a different setting and does not validate the main simulated and real-robot experiments.

Several statements do not agree with the reported tables. The paper says it improves over SAM3D on all reconstruction metrics except F@0.02 in the least-occluded regime, but Table 1 shows lower F-score in B1, B2, and B3, equality in B4, and an overall score of 0.189 versus 0.228. In the real-world table, it is also worse than SAM3D on both F-score and EMD. Table 1's SAM3D B3 normal consistency of 0.081 is likely erroneous given neighboring values near 0.8. These problems materially reduce confidence in the analysis and result verification.

The real-world evidence is too limited for the deployment and sim-to-real claims. It covers only five YCB objects already represented by their simulated counterparts, does not state the number of trials, provides no uncertainty or per-object breakdown, and does not explain how real-world ground-truth geometry and pose were obtained and aligned for quantitative evaluation. The qualitative figure itself contains a substantial calibration-induced failure.

The baseline protocol is insufficiently controlled and documented. It is unclear how SAM3D and Amodal3R receive masks, scale, alignment, and other task-specific inputs, or whether they are adapted comparably. The paper's own Vision-Only variant is dramatically weaker than SAM3D, making it difficult to separate multimodal benefits from differences in backbone, training data, and task adaptation. Comparisons with human-hand methods are performed on a separate dataset and are not a substitute for controlled comparisons in the principal setting.

Results are computed only on 'valid output meshes,' but validity rates are not reported for the main methods. This can introduce selection bias, especially when comparing generative systems with different failure rates. The number of sampling seeds used for quantitative averages is also omitted, and no variance or confidence intervals are provided.

The physical-guidance contribution appears modest in the reported ablation: removing inference guidance changes CD only from 0.033 to 0.036, while no direct physical metric is reported to show that guidance reduces penetration or improves contact. Consequently, its claimed importance rests mainly on a single qualitative trajectory.

The same Structure-VAE encoder and decoder trained on object SDFs appear to be used to encode and decode robot hands for the physical losses. The paper does not report hand-SDF reconstruction accuracy or justify that this object-trained latent model preserves thin fingers and inter-finger gaps. Errors here could corrupt both conditioning and the purported physical constraints.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Important architecture dimensions, model capacities, loss weights, optimizer and schedule details, guidance parameters, training duration, exact dataset splits, deduplication against YCB, mask acquisition at real-world inference, and seed counts are missing. Stage B is described only at a high level, and the SAM3D integration is characterized as preliminary.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: latent flow-based 3D reconstruction, SDF regularization, vision-touch fusion, contact/non-interpenetration objectives, and gradient guidance all have close precedents. The main novelty is their combination in this setting, so especially rigorous physical and real-world validation is needed. Overall, the work has promise, but the reporting inconsistencies and missing evidence for its defining claim favor rejection in its current form.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General. The manuscript presents a technically coherent multimodal reconstruction pipeline that combines camera-aligned metric SDFs, proprioceptive hand geometry, multi-contact touch, flow matching, and differentiable physical guidance. The work addresses an important computer-vision and robotics problem: single-view amodal reconstruction under severe hand occlusion, where vision-only shape priors can produce geometrically plausible but physically unusable outputs. Encoding positive contact evidence and negative free-space/interpenetration constraints in a shared 3D frame is well motivated and practically valuable.

Simulation evidence is broad and generally convincing. Evaluation covers 36 unseen YCB objects and 22,680 images, is stratified by occlusion, and uses several geometry and pose metrics. The method improves markedly over Amodal3R and is especially stronger than SAM3D in heavily occluded bins; the pose comparison is favorable even though SAM3D receives ground-truth depth-derived point maps.

The ablations are informative: vision-only, no-touch, training without physics losses, inference without guidance, and alternative contact encodings help isolate the contributions. Robustness tests for mask, tactile, and kinematic perturbations also connect the simulation study to deployment conditions.

Real-robot experiments on an unseen end-effector and the additional DexYCB human-hand evaluation provide meaningful evidence of cross-embodiment transfer. The reported 99% DexYCB reconstruction rate, strong F-scores, and low intersection volume are particularly encouraging.

The paper is clearly organized, gives explicit mathematical definitions of the main losses and guidance procedure, discusses calibration and grid-resolution limitations candidly, and includes useful qualitative results showing characteristic failures as well as successes.
weaknesses: The central claim is physical consistency, yet the main experiments report conventional reconstruction and pose metrics rather than direct contact error, penetration volume/rate, collision feasibility, or downstream manipulation success. The ablations support the claim indirectly, but direct physical metrics—especially separated by occlusion level—would make the scientific case substantially stronger.

The real-world evaluation is limited to five objects, and the manuscript does not clearly state the number of trials or samples represented in Table 3, provide dispersion or confidence intervals, or fully explain how real-world ground-truth geometry and pose were obtained. Consequently, the strength of the sim-to-real conclusion is difficult to judge statistically.

Baseline coverage is imperfect. The main comparisons are principally against vision-only systems that lack the additional proprioceptive and tactile information available to the proposed method, so some advantage is expected. Relevant hand-object methods are evaluated only through a separate DexYCB protocol, and there is no comparably equipped multimodal or test-time constraint-optimization baseline to isolate the benefit of the proposed learned formulation.

Reproducibility is weaker than the conceptual exposition: key architecture sizes, optimizer and schedule details, loss weights, guidance coefficients and stabilization settings, number of sampling steps, number of quantitative seeds, and code-release information are absent or insufficiently specified.

The fixed 64-cubed shared grid limits thin structures and concavities and reduces effective object resolution when the hand occupies much of the volume. Runtime is also nontrivial—approximately 18 seconds for both stages on an RTX A6000—which may restrict closed-loop robotic use.

There are minor presentation issues that should be corrected, including apparent numerical or typographical errors such as SAM3D's B3 normal consistency of 0.081 in Table 1 and several proofreading errors in the supplement. These do not materially undermine the contribution.
